solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Delta knocking 20 per cent off drink

parts.note: a delta is where a river meets the sea: a river mouth
RI, two of the ten letters, removed

explanation.surface: An airline passenger notices that Delta has cut the price of drinks by a fifth.
explanation.walkthrough: Delta reads as the airline, or the letter D in the NATO alphabet; it is the mouth of a river, and the percentage is worked out on the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermouth is a fortified, flavoured wine drunk as an aperitif.

clue.text: One seen climbing across building receiving rapier wound

indicators.note: wound as in twisted round, so the letters are coiled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

explanation.surface: A climber scaling a building is run through by a rapier and wounded.
explanation.walkthrough: "Wound" reads as an injury from the rapier; it is the past tense of wind. The definition is the long first half: the plant that covers house walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia creeper is a climbing vine often grown over the walls of buildings.

clue.text: Went through again to bowl, having changed ends

indicators.note: the first and last letters of the word swap places, as cricket teams change ends

parts.note: in cricket, to deliver the ball is to bowl it

explanation.surface: A cricketer bowls after the teams have switched ends.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bowler delivers the ball. 'having changed ends' swaps the D at the front of DELIVER with the R at its back.
explanation.definitionFit: To relive an experience is to go through it again in memory or imagination.

clue.text: Signs of Gallic strongman losing vote

indicators.note: the vote letter is dropped from the name

parts.note: Obelix, Asterix's menhir-carrying friend in the French comic
you mark a ballot with an X
OBELIX without X

explanation.surface: A French strongman is shown the signs that he has lost an election.
explanation.walkthrough: An obelus (plural obeli) is the dagger or division sign used in old manuscripts and printing.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeli are the dagger marks or division signs used in texts.

clue.text: Problem for choppers, heart of wood breaking defective hatchet

indicators.note: one piece breaks into the other, so it is inserted
a defective item is faulty, so its letters are out of order

parts.note: the word as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letters

parts.note: its two middle letters are OO

explanation.surface: The core of a log splits a faulty little axe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Choppers' are teeth, not axes, despite the hatchet. 'heart of' gives the middle OO of wood, which goes 'breaking' into HATCHET rearranged by 'defective'.
explanation.definitionFit: Choppers is slang for teeth, and a pain in the teeth is the trouble they suffer.

clue.text: Get off sled, perhaps, in downpour

parts.note: de- is the prefix for removing, as in de-plane
a luge is a racing sled

explanation.surface: A tobogganer is told to climb off the sled when it starts pouring.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is to read DELUGE as a made-up verb, de-luge, meaning to get off a luge, just as deplane means to leave an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name rain falling in a flood, and deluge can also stretch to any overwhelming rush.

clue.text: Quote half-hearted English novelist about having vigour

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: to cite is to quote

indicators.note: the novelist's name loses one of its two central letters, half its heart

parts.note: Graham Greene was the English novelist of Brighton Rock

explanation.surface: Someone quotes a lukewarm English author on the subject of being lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' takes one of the two middle Es out of GREENE, giving GRENE; 'about' then reverses CITE plus GRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: An energetic person is full of vitality and drive, so the adjective describes someone with vigour.

clue.text: Tense? Let go

definitions.meaning: tense = taut, the opposite of slack; the question mark flags a made-up reading

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first sense as a joke: tense means not loose, so un-loose. The real word means the opposite, to loosen or release.
explanation.definitionFit: To unloose something is to let it go or set it free.

clue.text: Old love letter perhaps being dismissed by church authorities

parts.note: ex = former
a love letter is one kind of communication

explanation.surface: A priest's old love letter turns up and he is thrown out by his bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a love letter got a clergyman sacked; "perhaps" marks the love letter as just one example of the wider word.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun phrase for the formal act: the church expels a member, cutting them off from its sacraments.

clue.text: Employed boss at NYT?

parts.note: the New York Times is an American paper
the editor, the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person was hired by the New York Times's boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition by example: the boss at the New York Times is an American editor, US ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Employed and used both mean put to work.

clue.text: Olivier developed work of some depth

indicators.note: developed as in worked into a new form

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Laurence Olivier developed a performance with real depth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Olivier's acting; rilievo is Italian for relief sculpture, carved out from a background to a certain depth.
explanation.definitionFit: Rilievo is relief sculpture, a work standing out to some depth from its ground.

clue.text: Old record producer's name recalled by woman

indicators.note: by means next to, so the reversed word sits beside the woman

parts.note: she stands for a woman

indicators.note: re-called reads as called back, so the word is turned round

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A woman remembers the name of a veteran music producer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns CALL into LLAC, placed 'by' SHE. Old 78 rpm gramophone records were made of shellac, the resin that 'produced' them; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellac, a resin made from insect secretions, was the material pressed into early gramophone discs.

clue.text: Attack in speech? Did just that

definitions.meaning: looks like a question about how to describe an attack; it is a definition of a verb meaning to rail against
asks for that verb in the past tense: someone who has already done it

explanation.walkthrough: The first half defines the verb INVEIGH, and the second asks for the past tense: someone who did just that inveighed.
explanation.definitionFit: To inveigh is to speak out violently against something, so inveighed is attacked in speech.

clue.text: Man of the match in space on heading in goal

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece on another follows it
the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is G
room means space

explanation.surface: A footballer heads in a goal and is named best player.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface misleads: the match is a wedding, and its man is the bridegroom. 'heading in' gives G, with ROOM 'on' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding is a match, and the groom is the man being married at it.

clue.text: List where cards are in report

indicators.note: report = something spoken, so we go by sound

parts.note: playing cards are kept in decks

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a list saying where the cards are, according to a report.
explanation.walkthrough: An index can be a card index, which makes the surface feel like office filing.
explanation.definitionFit: An index is an alphabetical list, as at the back of a book.

clue.text: Times tips for Brighton and Epsom include rank no-hope outsiders I fear

indicators.note: the outer letters include the other piece, holding it inside
and simply joins the two tips, the second following the first

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as times

indicators.note: the tips of words are their first letters

parts.note: its first letter is B
its tip, the first letter, is E, under the same 'tips for'

indicators.note: rank means foul, so the letters are spoilt and jumbled

parts.note: the letters as written, NOHOPE

explanation.surface: A racing tipster dismisses rank outsiders at Brighton and Epsom racecourses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips for' gives B and E; 'rank' jumbles NOHOPE into ENOPHO, which X, B and E 'include'. The definition is the person speaking: someone who says 'outsiders I fear'.
explanation.definitionFit: A xenophobe is a person with a dread or hatred of foreigners and strangers.

clue.text: Exercise caution re drink

indicators.note: to exercise is to work, and the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Advice to go carefully with alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: "Exercise caution" is a stock phrase, which hides that exercise is the instruction and caution the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a French orange liqueur is one brand of drink.

clue.text: Messy, I'd clean it all the same

indicators.note: a mess of letters to be tidied into a word

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that, however messy the thing is, they would clean it anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: "All the same" reads as "nevertheless" in the surface; it is the definition, meaning exactly alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: all the same, read as an adjective phrase, means matching in every detail.

clue.text: Conservative set defending right to property for patrons

indicators.note: the outer letters surround and guard the right

parts.note: C = Conservative, TELE = a television set
a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: A Conservative group defends property rights on behalf of its patrons.
explanation.walkthrough: "Set" reads as a group of Conservatives, but it is a television set; tele is an old British word for a TV.
explanation.definitionFit: A collective noun matching a plural: the whole body of a shop's regular customers.

clue.text: To gratify member of ruling party, expected to embrace flag regularly

parts.note: a party that is in is in power, so its member is in

indicators.note: the outer word embraces the other piece, holding it inside

parts.note: due means expected

indicators.note: regularly means alternate letters are taken

parts.note: its alternate letters L and G

explanation.surface: A government loyalist is expected to wave the national flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second and fourth letters of flag, LG, which DUE is 'to embrace'.
explanation.definitionFit: To indulge someone is to give in to their wishes, satisfying or pleasing them.

clue.text: Sign crop's failing for island

indicators.note: a failing crop is lost, so that word is taken away

parts.note: Capricorn is a sign of the zodiac
corn is a crop; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A harvest failing is taken as an omen for an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing' takes CORN off the end of CAPRICORN. Capri is an Italian island in the Bay of Naples.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is a small island off the coast of Campania in southern Italy.

clue.text: I study South American nation's former queen

parts.note: Peru
the possessive S
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A historian studies a former queen of a South American country.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken by the answer: a peruser is someone who can say "I study". ER is now a former queen because Elizabeth II has died.
explanation.definitionFit: A peruser reads or studies something carefully, so "I study" is what one would say.

clue.text: Finally find oneself back in the saddle

parts.note: the back end of something
a jockey who is riding is up

explanation.surface: A rider eventually finds themself back on the horse.
explanation.walkthrough: "Back in the saddle" is a set phrase for returning to work, so it hides that the two halves work separately; racing reports say a jockey is up when riding.
explanation.definitionFit: To end up somewhere is to finally find yourself there.

clue.text: Suffering clergyman and agents scratching heads — what's causing rash?

indicators.note: to scratch is to strike out, so the head of each word is crossed off

parts.note: hurt means suffering
a vicar is a parish clergyman; with its head scratched too it leaves ICAR
the CIA is the US intelligence agency; with its head scratched too it leaves IA

explanation.surface: A vicar and some spies are in distress, puzzling over what brought on a skin complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching heads' removes the first letter of each of HURT, VICAR and CIA, leaving URT, ICAR and IA. Scratching is also what a rash makes you do.
explanation.definitionFit: Urticaria, also called hives or nettle rash, is the skin condition that produces itchy weals.

clue.text: Ready for university, turn over a new leaf

parts.note: U = university
PTO, please turn over, is written at the foot of a page to send you to the next leaf

explanation.surface: A student ready for university resolves to make a fresh start.
explanation.walkthrough: "Turn over a new leaf" is an idiom for reforming; here it is literal, turning a page, which is what PTO asks.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to a task means ready for it or capable of it.

clue.text: Bellyache about cops removing clothing

parts.note: c = circa, about
POLICE without its outer letters

explanation.surface: Someone complains about police officers stripping off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bellyache" reads as a verb, to complain; it is the noun, a pain in the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Colic is severe abdominal pain, a bellyache.

clue.text: Withdrawal — drink not an option

parts.note: a pull is a swig from a bottle or glass
an idea that is out is ruled out

explanation.surface: Someone in withdrawal is told that drinking is no longer an option.
explanation.walkthrough: "Withdrawal" reads as a recovering drinker's symptoms; it is the military sense, an army leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the military sense: troops leaving a region.

clue.text: Company beginning to implode after mislaying substantial figures

indicators.note: the last piece comes after the one before it in the answer

parts.note: loss is the act of mislaying something

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is I

explanation.surface: A firm starts to collapse after losing some major players.
explanation.walkthrough: The business surface hides statues: 'substantial figures' are giant sculptures, and the plural is Latin. 'beginning to' gives the I of implode, which comes 'after' LOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Colossi, plural of colossus, are huge statues such as the one that stood at Rhodes.

clue.text: Colour associated with sea in which fish swam

indicators.note: the fish goes in the colour

parts.note: the Red Sea
an eel is a fish

explanation.surface: A painter chooses a sea colour in which fish are swimming.
explanation.walkthrough: "Swam" belongs to the fish in the surface; it means a head that swam, dizzy, i.e. reeled.
explanation.definitionFit: When your head swims or reels, you feel giddy.

clue.text: Put Reagan in power? It's a little bit charged

parts.note: put … in power = voted into office; the phrase is split around Reagan
Ronald Reagan, US president, was Ron

explanation.surface: Voting Ronald Reagan into office was, as it turned out, somewhat controversial.
explanation.walkthrough: "Charged" suggests a politically charged decision; the definition means a tiny particle carrying an electric charge.
explanation.definitionFit: An electron is a tiny subatomic particle with a negative charge.
